mainTopic: Stories of merit and shaky buildings (רבי יוחנן and אילפא, נחום איש גם זו), and the definition of a plague (דבר)
overview: The amud opens with the last words of an earlier statement: one practice could not be kept in מחוזא because the city had so many soldiers. Then come stories about shaky buildings. אילפא and רבי יוחנן left their learning to do business, and while they sat under a crumbling wall, רבי יוחנן overheard angels sparing them only because one of them still had a great future. רבי יוחנן went back to learning and became head of the academy. אילפא later proved he had not forgotten his Torah by explaining a hard ברייתא through רבי מאיר's rule that it is a מצוה to carry out the words of the dead. Next, נחום איש גם זו, who was terribly afflicted, kept a falling house standing by his merit. He explained that his suffering was his own request after a poor man died while he made him wait. The גמרא then explains his name with the story of the stolen gift of jewels, where he said גם זו לטובה and everything turned out for the good. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה and uses a ברייתא to define a plague (דבר) by the size of a city and the pattern of deaths over three days.

steps.title: Why one practice could not be kept in מחוזא
steps.stepSummary: The closing words of an earlier statement: the reason is that there are many soldiers in מחוזא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because there are many soldiers in מחוזא.
steps.whatsHappening: These words finish a statement that began earlier on the page. They give the reason why one practice could not be followed in the city of מחוזא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason given is that מחוזא was full of soldiers. Opening one's home to everyone there would not work. Only the reason itself appears in this section, so it closes the earlier discussion before a new story begins.

keyTerms.meaning: מחוזא, a large Jewish city in Babylonia

phrases.english: Because there are many
soldiers in מחוזא.
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence that started earlier on the page. If he let everyone in to eat, the soldiers would eat up all his food.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דִּנְפִישִׁי בְּנֵי חֵילָא דְּמָחוֹזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a statement that began before this section
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: One practice could not be kept in מחוזא because of the large number of soldiers there.

steps.title: Two poor scholars decide to go into business
steps.stepSummary: אילפא and רבי יוחנן are learning Torah and become very poor, so they decide to go into business.
steps.simpleTranslation: אילפא and רבי יוחנן were learning Torah, and money became very tight for them. They said: Let us get up, go, do business, and fulfill for ourselves the פסוק 'However, there shall be no needy among you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story. Two Torah scholars are so poor that they decide to leave their learning and earn a living.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They use a פסוק to support their plan: 'there shall be no needy among you.' They read it as a reason to stop being poor. The story will test whether this was the right choice.

keyTerms.meaning: Things were very hard for them, meaning they were very poor

phrases.english: אילפא and רבי יוחנן
were learning Torah,
and things became very hard for them,
They said: Let us get up and go
and do business
and fulfill for ourselves
'However, there shall be no needy among you.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילְפָא וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֲווֹ גָּרְסִי בְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new story after the earlier discussion ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two struggling scholars decide to leave Torah study for business, using a פסוק as support.

steps.title: Eating under a crumbling wall when angels arrive
steps.stepSummary: On the way, they sit and eat under a shaky wall, and two ministering angels arrive.
steps.simpleTranslation: They went and sat under a crumbling wall. They were eating bread, and two ministering angels came.
steps.whatsHappening: The story sets the scene for what comes next. The two scholars sit under a dangerous wall, and angels appear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shaky wall matters because the angels will talk about knocking it down. This step prepares the main event of the story.

phrases.english: They went and sat
under a crumbling wall,
and they were eating bread,
and two ministering angels came.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲזַלוּ, אוֹתִיבוּ תּוּתֵי גּוּדָּא רְעִיעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by setting the scene
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The scholars sit under a dangerous wall, and angels appear.

steps.title: The angels discuss whether to kill them
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן overhears one angel wanting to kill them for leaving Torah. The other angel says to leave them, because one of them still has a great future.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן heard one angel say to the other: Let us throw this wall on them and kill them, because they are leaving eternal life and busying themselves with temporary life. The other said: Leave them, because one of them has his hour still waiting for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The angels argue about the two scholars. One wants to punish them, and the other wants to spare them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first angel calls Torah 'eternal life' and business 'temporary life.' Leaving Torah for business is presented as a serious failing. The second angel does not argue with that. He only says one of them is destined for greatness, so they should be spared.

keyTerms.meaning: Eternal life, the life of the World to Come, meaning Torah study
Temporary life, meaning earning a living
His hour is still waiting for him, meaning his greatness is still to come

steps.confusionAlert: The second angel does not say leaving Torah was fine. He only says to spare them because one of them has a great future ahead.

phrases.english: רבי יוחנן heard
one say to the other:
Let us throw this wall on them
and kill them,
because they are leaving eternal life
and busying themselves with temporary life!
The other said to him: Leave them,
because there is one of them
whose hour is still waiting for him.
phrases.notes: He means his time of greatness has not come yet, so he cannot die now.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁמְעֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאָמַר חַד לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Describes what the angels from step 3 said
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Leaving Torah for business is seen as leaving eternal life. They are spared only because one of them is destined for greatness.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main lesson of the story: how much Torah study is valued compared with earning a living.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן figures out the future is his
steps.stepSummary: Only רבי יוחנן heard the angels. From this he concludes that he is the one with the great future.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן heard, but אילפא did not. רבי יוחנן asked אילפא: Did you hear anything? He said: No. רבי יוחנן said: Since I heard and אילפא did not, this shows that I am the one whose hour is waiting for me.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן checks whether אילפא also heard the angels. When אילפא says no, רבי יוחנן draws a conclusion about himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reasoning is simple. The message was meant for the one who heard it. Since only he heard, the angel's words about 'one of them' must refer to him.

keyTerms.meaning: Did you hear anything? (מָר is a respectful 'you')

phrases.english: רבי יוחנן heard,
but אילפא did not hear.
רבי יוחנן said to אילפא:
Did the master hear anything?
He said to him: No.
He said: Since I heard
and אילפא did not hear,
learn from this
that it is for me that the hour is waiting.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדִּשְׁמַעִי אֲנָא וְאִילְפָא לָא שְׁמַע, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Works out which of the two the angel meant in step 4
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוחנן is the one destined for greatness
steps.raayaSupportSource: Only רבי יוחנן heard the angels; אילפא did not

steps.title: רבי יוחנן returns to Torah and becomes the leader
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן goes back to learning, quoting a different פסוק. אילפא keeps going. By the time אילפא returns, רבי יוחנן has been appointed head.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said to אילפא: I will go back and fulfill for myself 'For the needy will never cease from the land.' רבי יוחנן went back, and אילפא did not. By the time אילפא came back, רבי יוחנן had been appointed head.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. רבי יוחנן chooses Torah over business, and he is rewarded with leadership.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן swaps פסוקים. Instead of 'there shall be no needy,' he now accepts 'the needy will never cease,' meaning he is ready to stay poor for the sake of Torah. אילפא continues in business, and when he returns, רבי יוחנן has already risen to lead the academy.
steps.whatToRemember: The two פסוקים frame the whole story. At first the scholars wanted to escape poverty ('there shall be no needy'). רבי יוחנן ended up accepting poverty for Torah ('the needy will never cease'), and his great future came true.

phrases.english: רבי יוחנן said to him: I will go back,
and fulfill for myself
'For the needy will never cease from the land.'
רבי יוחנן went back,
but אילפא did not go back.
By the time אילפא came back,
רבי יוחנן had been appointed head.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֶיהֱדַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Acts on the conclusion of step 5 and reverses the plan from step 2
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יוחנן chose Torah over business, accepting poverty, and he rose to lead the academy as the angel had said.

steps.title: אילפא's friends say he missed his chance
steps.stepSummary: When אילפא comes back, his colleagues tell him that if he had stayed and learned, he would have been the one appointed head.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: If the Master had stayed and learned, wouldn't the Master have been appointed head?
steps.whatsHappening: אילפא's colleagues point out that he could have been appointed instead of רבי יוחנן if he had kept learning. This sets up אילפא's dramatic response in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 ended with רבי יוחנן already appointed. Now the people around אילפא make the painful point out loud: the job went to the one who stayed. The question is not really asking for information. It is a sharp remark that pushes אילפא to prove himself.

keyTerms.meaning: the Master, a respectful way of saying 'you'

phrases.english: They said to him:
If the Master had sat and learned,
wouldn't the Master have been appointed head?
phrases.notes: Read this as a question that expects a yes: you would have been appointed!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אִי אִתִּיב מָר וְגָרֵיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the result in step 6, where רבי יוחנן was appointed head while אילפא was away.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Had אילפא stayed in the בית מדרש, he would have been appointed head.

steps.title: אילפא hangs from the mast and challenges everyone
steps.stepSummary: אילפא hangs from a ship's mast and declares that he will fall and drown if anyone asks him about a ברייתא of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא that he cannot explain from a משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and hung himself from the mast of a ship. He said: If anyone asks me about a ברייתא of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא and I cannot answer it from a משנה, I will fall from the ship's mast and drown.
steps.whatsHappening: אילפא answers his friends with a dramatic act. He hangs from a ship's mast and offers to be tested on hard ברייתות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אילפא wants to show that his time in business did not make him forget his learning. His challenge is very hard: he must explain any ברייתא of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא using only a משנה. He puts his life on the line to prove it.

keyTerms.meaning: a ברייתא, a teaching left out of the משנה

phrases.english: He went and hung himself
from the mast of a ship,
he said: If there is anyone who asks me
about a ברייתא of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya
and I do not answer it for him from a משנה,
I will fall from the mast of the ship
and drown.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲזַל תְּלָא נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּאַסְקַרְיָא דִסְפִינְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: אילפא's response to his friends' remark in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אילפא claims he can explain any ברייתא of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא from a משנה.

steps.title: An old man tests אילפא with a case about a dying man's instructions
steps.stepSummary: An old man quotes a ברייתא about a father who tells people to give his sons a שקל every week. It lists when the sons get more and when they get only a שקל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain old man came and taught him: If someone says, 'Give my sons a שקל each week,' and they really need a סלע, they give them a סלע. But if he said, 'Give them only a שקל,' they give them only a שקל. If he said, 'If they die, others will inherit in their place,' then whether he said 'give' or 'give only,' they give them only a שקל.
steps.whatsHappening: An old man accepts אילפא's challenge and quotes a ברייתא for him to explain. This sets up אילפא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has three cases. If the father just said 'a שקל,' we assume he meant 'whatever they need,' so they may get a סלע. If he said 'only a שקל,' or he made it clear that others inherit after his sons, the money is meant to be saved, so the sons get only a שקל. The test is to find which משנה-level principle explains all of this.

keyTerms.meaning: a coin, half of a סלע
others will inherit in their place

steps.confusionAlert: בְּשַׁבָּת here does not mean 'on שבת.' It means 'per week,' an allowance given each week.

phrases.english: A certain old man came and taught him:
One who says: Give my sons a shekel each week,
and they are fit to be given a sela,
they give them a sela.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אָמַר: אַל תִּתְּנוּ לָהֶם אֶלָּא שֶׁקֶל
phrases.english: But if he said: Do not give them more than a shekel,
they give them only a shekel.
If he said: If they die,
others will inherit in their place,
whether he said "give"
or he said "do not give" more,
they give them only a shekel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא הָהוּא סָבָא, תְּנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The old man takes up the challenge אילפא made in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which source or opinion explains this ברייתא about a dying man's instructions for his sons?

steps.title: אילפא explains the case according to רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: אילפא answers that the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר, who holds that it is a מצוה to carry out the words of a person who has died.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Whose view is this? It is רבי מאיר, who said: It is a מצוה to fulfill the words of the dead.
steps.whatsHappening: אילפא passes the test. He shows that the whole ברייתא rests on one principle of רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every case in the ברייתא is about doing exactly what the dead father really wanted. When he wanted his sons provided for, they get what they need. When he wanted the money saved for others, they get only a שקל. All of it comes from רבי מאיר's rule that we must carry out the words of the dead.

keyTerms.meaning: it is a מצוה to carry out the wishes of the dead

steps.whatToRemember: אילפא proved that even after leaving to do business, he could still tie a hard ברייתא back to one clear principle: מצוה לקיים דברי המת, following רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: He said to him: Whose view is this?
phrases.notes: אילפא is the one speaking now, answering the old man.

phrases.english: It is Rabbi Meir, who said:
It is a מצוה to fulfill the words of the dead.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָא מַנִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the old man's test from step 9 and so fulfills אילפא's challenge from step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא follows רבי מאיר: מצוה לקיים דברי המת.

steps.title: נחום איש גם זו's great suffering
steps.stepSummary: A new story begins. נחום איש גם זו was blind, missing his arms and legs, and covered in boils. He lay in a shaky house with the legs of his bed in buckets of water to keep ants away.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said about נחום איש גם זו that he was blind in both eyes, missing both arms, missing both legs, and his whole body was full of boils. He lay in a shaky house, and the legs of his bed were set in buckets of water so ants would not climb onto him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story and first describes נחום איש גם זו and his condition. This sets the scene for what happens with the house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the shaky wall in step 3, this story is about a building that could fall at any moment. The details show how much נחום suffered: he could not even brush ants off himself. The scene is set so we will see what kept the house standing.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ עָלָיו עַל נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ
phrases.english: They said about Nachum of Gam Zu
that he was blind in both his eyes,
missing both his arms,
missing both his legs,
and his whole body was full of boils.
And he was lying in a shaky house,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַגְלֵי מִטָּתוֹ מוּנָּחִין בִּסְפָלִין שֶׁל מַיִם
phrases.english: and the legs of his bed were set in buckets of water
so that ants would not climb onto him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ עָלָיו עַל נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story, linked to the earlier one by the theme of a shaky building that stays standing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נחום איש גם זו suffered terribly and lived in a house that was about to fall.

steps.title: נחום tells his students to take out his bed last
steps.stepSummary: His students want to carry out his bed first, but נחום tells them to take out the things first, because the house will not fall while he is inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once his students wanted to take out his bed first and the things afterward. He said to them: My sons, take out the things first and my bed afterward, because you can be sure that as long as I am in the house, the house will not fall.
steps.whatsHappening: The students try to save their teacher first. נחום tells them to reverse the order because his presence protects the house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students thought the person matters most, so he should come out first. נחום knew the house was standing only because of his merit. If they took him out first, it would collapse before the things could be saved.

keyTerms.meaning: you can be sure, it is guaranteed to you

phrases.english: Once his students wanted
to take out his bed,
and afterward take out the things.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: בָּנַיי, פַּנּוּ אֶת הַכֵּלִים,
phrases.english: He said to them: My sons, take out the things,
and afterward take out my bed,
for you can be sure
that as long as I am in the house
the house will not fall.

steps.triggerLanguage: פַּעַם אַחַת בִּקְּשׁוּ תַּלְמִידָיו לְפַנּוֹת מִטָּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the scene from step 11 with the shaky house.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: As long as נחום is in the house, it will not fall.

steps.title: The house falls right after נחום is carried out
steps.stepSummary: The students take out the things and then his bed, and right away the house falls.
steps.simpleTranslation: They took out the things and afterward took out his bed, and the house fell.
steps.whatsHappening: The students follow נחום's instructions, and the moment he is out, the house collapses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This proves נחום's words true. The house was standing only because of his merit, and it fell as soon as he left. This connects back to the theme of a righteous person's merit protecting the place where he is.
steps.whatToRemember: The merit of a great צדיק like נחום איש גם זו can hold up a falling building, just as the merit of a future great person kept the shaky wall from hurting אילפא and רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: They took out the things
and afterward took out his bed,
and the house fell.

steps.triggerLanguage: פִּינּוּ אֶת הַכֵּלִים וְאַחַר כָּךְ פִּינּוּ אֶת מִטָּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that נחום's promise in step 12 came true.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The house stood only because of נחום's merit and fell as soon as he was carried out.

steps.title: The students ask why a righteous man suffers
steps.stepSummary: After seeing that the house did not fall while he was inside, the students ask נחום why someone so righteous has such terrible suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: His students said to him: רבי, since you are a completely righteous man, why did this happen to you?
steps.whatsHappening: The students ask a question that comes straight out of the story of the falling house. This sets up נחום's personal explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The house falling right after he left showed that he was a צדיק גמור. So his suffering seems hard to understand, and the students want to know the reason.

phrases.english: His students said to him:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי, וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר אַתָּה,
phrases.english: Rabbi, since you are a completely righteous man,
why has this happened to you?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ תַּלְמִידָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The miracle of the house in Step 13 shows he is a צדיק, which raises the question of why he suffers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a completely righteous person has such great suffering.

steps.title: I brought it on myself: the poor man who died
steps.stepSummary: נחום explains that once, on the way to his father-in-law, a poor man asked him for food. He told him to wait until he unloaded the donkey, and the poor man died before he finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: My sons, I caused it myself. Once I was traveling to my father-in-law's house with three donkeys loaded with food, drink, and treats. A poor man stood in my way and said, 'רבי, feed me.' I told him, 'Wait until I unload the donkey.' Before I could finish unloading, he died.
steps.whatsHappening: נחום answers his students by telling a story from his own life. He says his suffering is his own doing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He had plenty of food with him, yet he delayed helping the poor man for a short moment. That delay ended with the man's death, and נחום holds himself responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: Kinds of delicacies or sweet treats
His soul left him; he died

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: בָּנַיי, אֲנִי גָּרַמְתִּי לְעַצְמִי.
phrases.english: He said to them: My sons, I brought it upon myself.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁפַּעַם אַחַת הָיִיתִי מְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ לְבֵית חָמִי,
phrases.english: For once I was traveling on the road to my father-in-law's house,
and I had with me a load of three donkeys,

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד שֶׁל מַאֲכָל, וְאֶחָד שֶׁל מִשְׁתֶּה,
phrases.english: one of food, and one of drink,
and one of delicacies.

phrases.aramaic: בָּא עָנִי אֶחָד וְעָמַד לִי בַּדֶּרֶךְ,
phrases.english: A poor man came and stood before me on the road,
and said to me: My rabbi, sustain me.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַרְתִּי לוֹ: הַמְתֵּן עַד שֶׁאֶפְרוֹק מִן הַחֲמוֹר.
phrases.english: I said to him: Wait until I unload the donkey.
I did not manage to unload the donkey
before his soul left him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: בָּנַיי, אֲנִי גָּרַמְתִּי לְעַצְמִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the students' question from Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His suffering came because of his own failure to help a starving poor man right away.

steps.title: נחום asks for his body to be afflicted
steps.stepSummary: נחום falls on the dead man's face and asks that his eyes, hands, and legs be struck, matching the ways he failed the poor man. He finally asks that his whole body be covered with boils.
steps.simpleTranslation: I went and fell on his face and said: My eyes, which had no pity on your eyes, should go blind. My hands, which had no pity on your hands, should be cut off. My legs, which had no pity on your legs, should be cut off. And I was not at peace until I said: My whole body should be full of boils.
steps.whatsHappening: נחום continues his story and explains how each part of his suffering began. This connects back to how he was described in Step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each body part matches the failure: eyes that saw the poor man, hands that could have given, and legs that could have hurried. This explains exactly the four sufferings from Step 11: blindness, no arms, no legs, and boils.

keyTerms.meaning: My mind was settled; I was at peace

phrases.english: I went and fell upon his face, and said:

phrases.aramaic: עֵינַי שֶׁלֹּא חָסוּ עַל עֵינֶיךָ — יִסּוֹמוּ,
phrases.english: My eyes, which had no pity on your eyes, should be blinded;

phrases.aramaic: יָדַיי שֶׁלֹּא חָסוּ עַל יָדֶיךָ — יִתְגַּדְּמוּ,
phrases.english: my hands, which had no pity on your hands, should be cut off;

phrases.aramaic: רַגְלַי שֶׁלֹּא חָסוּ עַל רַגְלֶיךָ — יִתְקַטְּעוּ.
phrases.english: my legs, which had no pity on your legs, should be cut off.
And my mind did not rest until I said:
My whole body should be full of boils.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָלַכְתִּי וְנָפַלְתִּי עַל פָּנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the answer and links each suffering in Step 11 to his own request.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נחום himself asked for each suffering, measure for measure, for failing the poor man.

steps.title: Woe to us, and woe to me if not
steps.stepSummary: The students cry that it is painful to see him this way. נחום replies that it would be worse for him if they did not see him suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Woe to us that we see you like this! He said to them: Woe to me if you did not see me like this.
steps.whatsHappening: The conversation ends with a short exchange between the students and their teacher. This closes the story of נחום's suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students see only the pain. נחום sees the suffering as good for him, since it makes up for his failure, so without it he would be worse off.

keyTerms.meaning: You saw me in this state

steps.whatToRemember: נחום איש גם זו accepted his suffering with love. He saw it as making up for a delay in helping a poor man, so to him it was a good thing.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אוֹי לָנוּ שֶׁרְאִינוּךָ בְּכָךְ!
phrases.english: They said to him: Woe to us that we have seen you like this!

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: אוֹי לִי אִם לֹא רְאִיתוּנִי בְּכָךְ.
phrases.english: He said to them: Woe to me if you had not seen me like this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אוֹי לָנוּ שֶׁרְאִינוּךָ בְּכָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story by showing how נחום viewed his suffering.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Suffering that makes up for a wrong is good for the person, even though it hurts to look at.

steps.title: Why was he called נחום איש גם זו?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the name נחום איש גם זו comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did they call him נחום איש גם זו?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new question about this same person and asks about his name. This sets up the explanation and a new story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גם זו could sound like the name of a place. The גמרא wants to show that the name actually describes the way he thought.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַמַּאי קָרוּ לֵיהּ נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ —
phrases.english: And why did they call him Naḥum of Gam Zu?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַמַּאי קָרוּ לֵיהּ נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from his suffering to the meaning of his name.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for the name איש גם זו.

steps.title: Because he always said 'this too is for the good'
steps.stepSummary: Whatever happened to him, he would say גם זו לטובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because about anything that happened to him, he would say: This too is for the good.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about his name. Next it will tell a story that shows this attitude.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name comes from his habit of saying גם זו לטובה, not from a place. He said it about everything, including things that looked bad.

keyTerms.meaning: This too is for the good

phrases.english: Because about anything that happened to him,
he would say: This too is for the good.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּכׇל מִילְּתָא דַּהֲוָה סָלְקָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He was called איש גם זו because he always said גם זו לטובה.

steps.title: The jewels are stolen at the inn
steps.stepSummary: The Jews send נחום with a chest of jewels as a gift to the קיסר. At an inn, the people living there steal the jewels during the night and fill the chest with earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once the Jews wanted to send a gift to the emperor's palace. They said: Who should go? Let נחום איש גם זו go, because he is used to miracles. They sent with him a chest full of jewels and pearls. He went and slept at an inn. At night the people living there took everything from his chest and filled it with earth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story that shows how נחום always said גם זו לטובה. Here the trouble starts: the gift is stolen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He was chosen because he was used to miracles, which hints that a miracle will come. The swap of jewels for earth sets up a dangerous problem for when he reaches the king.

keyTerms.meaning: An inn, a place to stay

phrases.english: Once, the Jews wanted to send
a gift to the emperor's palace.
They said: Who should go?

phrases.aramaic: יֵיזִיל נַחוּם אִישׁ גַּם זוֹ, דִּמְלוּמָּד בְּנִיסִּין הוּא.
phrases.english: Let Naḥum of Gam Zu go, because he is used to miracles.
They sent with him a chest full
of jewels and pearls.
He went and spent the night at a certain inn.
During the night, those residents got up
and took everything from his chest and filled it with earth.

steps.triggerLanguage: זִימְנָא חֲדָא בְּעוֹ לְשַׁדּוֹרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דּוֹרוֹן לְבֵי קֵיסָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story that shows the attitude explained in Step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The jewels for the קיסר were stolen and replaced with earth.

steps.title: The king finds earth and wants to kill them
steps.stepSummary: At the palace the chest is opened and found full of earth. The king thinks the Jews are mocking him and wants to kill them all, yet נחום says גם זו לטובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he arrived there, they opened the chest and saw it was full of earth. The king wanted to kill them all. He said: The Jews are making fun of me. נחום said: This too is for the good.
steps.whatsHappening: The danger reaches its peak at the palace. Even facing death, נחום says his famous words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the theft looks like an insult to the king, and it puts the whole group in danger of death. נחום's גם זו לטובה here shows how deep his trust was.

keyTerms.meaning: They are laughing at me, mocking me

phrases.english: When he arrived there, they opened the chest,
and saw that it was full of earth.
The king wanted to kill all of them.
He said: The Jews are mocking me.
He said: This too is for the good.
phrases.notes: This speaker is נחום, not the king.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי מְטָא הָתָם, שְׁרִינְהוּ לְסִיפְטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The theft from Step 20 now leads to a death threat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facing death, נחום still says גם זו לטובה.

steps.title: אליהו suggests it is the earth of אברהם
steps.stepSummary: אליהו הנביא appears as one of the king's men and suggests the earth may be the special earth of אברהם אבינו, which turned into swords and arrows when thrown, as hinted in a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליהו came, looking like one of them, and said to the king: Maybe this earth is from the earth of their father אברהם. When he threw earth, it became swords, and when he threw straw, it became arrows, as it says: 'His sword makes them like dust, his bow like blown straw.'
steps.whatsHappening: The turnaround begins: אליהו offers the king a new way to see the earth. The story will go on to show whether it really works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What looked like an insult may actually be a powerful weapon. The פסוק from ישעיהו is read as speaking about אברהם, whose dust became swords and whose straw became arrows.

keyTerms.meaning: Appeared to him, took on the look of

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the start of the proof that גם זו לטובה: the theft that seemed like a disaster is about to become the reason for success.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתָא אֵלִיָּהוּ אִדְּמִי לֵיהּ כְּחַד מִינַּיְיהוּ,
phrases.english: Elijah came and appeared to him as one of them,
phrases.notes: He looked like one of the king's own officials.

phrases.english: and said to him: Perhaps this earth
is from the earth of their father Abraham.

phrases.aramaic: דְּכִי הֲוָה שָׁדֵי עַפְרָא — הָווּ סַיְיפֵי,
phrases.english: For when he threw earth, it became swords,
and when he threw straw, it became arrows,

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״יִתֵּן כֶּעָפָר חַרְבּוֹ כְּקַשׁ נִדָּף קַשְׁתּוֹ״.
phrases.english: as it is written: “His sword makes them as the dust, his bow as the driven stubble.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא אֵלִיָּהוּ אִדְּמִי לֵיהּ כְּחַד מִינַּיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a way out of the death threat in Step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אליהו suggests the earth is אברהם's miraculous earth, based on ישעיהו 41:2.

steps.title: The earth works, and נחום is sent home with treasure
steps.stepSummary: The earth from the chest is tested in battle. It conquers a province that could not be taken. The king's men fill נחום's chest with jewels and send him off with great honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was one province they had never been able to conquer. They tested some of the earth on it and conquered it. Then they went into the treasury, filled נחום's chest with precious stones and pearls, and sent him off with great honor.
steps.whatsHappening: The suggestion of אליהו from the last step is tried out, and it works. נחום's גם זו לטובה turns out to be true: the 'bad' earth saves the Jews and brings him great honor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the story was a disaster: stolen jewels and a king who wanted to kill everyone. Here it flips completely. The earth itself becomes the miracle, and the chest ends up fuller than when he left. This is the clearest picture of what גם זו לטובה means.

phrases.english: There was one province
that they were unable to conquer.
They tested some of it and conquered it.
phrases.notes: "Some of it" means some of the earth from נחום's chest, thrown at the enemy the way אליהו suggested.

phrases.english: They went into his treasury
and filled his chest
phrases.notes: The treasury is the king's, but the chest is נחום's.

phrases.english: with precious stones and pearls,
and sent him off with great honor.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַוְיָא חֲדָא מְדִינְתָּא דְּלָא מָצוּ לְמִיכְבְּשַׁהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the suggestion in step 22 really worked.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The earth turned out to be miraculous. נחום was rewarded with jewels and honor, which proves his גם זו לטובה true.

steps.title: The innkeepers ask נחום about his honor
steps.stepSummary: On the way home נחום stays at the same inn. The residents ask what he brought to get such honor, and he answers truthfully: what I took from here, I brought there.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they came back, they spent the night at that same inn. The residents asked him: What did you bring with you that they gave you so much honor? He told them: What I took from here, I brought there.
steps.whatsHappening: נחום comes back to the inn where his jewels were stolen. His honest answer makes the thieves think their own earth is magical.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחום does not lie, and he does not accuse them. His words are true: the earth they put into his chest is what he brought to the king. The innkeepers misread his answer, and that sets up their downfall in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: an inn, a place to lodge

phrases.english: When they came, they spent the night at that same inn.
They said to him:
What did you bring with you
that they gave you so much honor?
He said to them:
What I took from here
I brought there.
phrases.notes: His words are completely true, but the innkeepers hear them as "the earth from your inn made the miracle."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתוֹ, בִּיתוּ בְּהָהוּא דִּיּוּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows נחום on his way home, back to the inn from step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נחום answers truthfully that he brought there what he took from here, which leads the thieves to a wrong conclusion.

steps.title: The innkeepers bring their own earth and are punished
steps.stepSummary: The residents tear down their inn and bring its earth to the king, claiming the miracle earth came from them. It is tested and does nothing, so the king has them killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They tore down their house and brought its earth to the king's palace. They told him: That earth that was brought here came from us. The king tested it, it did nothing, and he had those residents killed.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the thieves punished. Their earth has no power at all, because the miracle came from נחום's merit and not from the dirt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same earth that saved נחום brings death to the people who stole from him. This shows the miracle was never about the earth itself. With this the story of נחום איש גם זו is finished.
steps.whatToRemember: The story shows גם זו לטובה in action. What looked like a disaster became נחום's salvation, and the thieves were punished by their own scheme.

phrases.english: They tore down their dwelling
and brought it to the king's palace.
phrases.notes: "It" means the earth from under their torn-down inn.

phrases.english: They said to him:
That earth that was brought here
is from ours.
They tested it and did not find it to work,
and they killed those residents.

steps.triggerLanguage: סְתַרוּ לְדִירַיְיהוּ וְאַמְטִינְהוּ לְבֵי מַלְכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows what came of the innkeepers misreading נחום's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The innkeepers' earth has no power, and they are killed. The miracle belonged to נחום alone.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: what counts as a plague
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves the stories and quotes the משנה's definition of דבר: a city that sends out five hundred foot-soldiers, and so on.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: What is a plague? A city that sends out five hundred foot-soldiers, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is returning to the משנה after the long story section. It quotes the line about דבר to set up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave one case: a city of five hundred men with three deaths over three days in a row. By quoting it again, the גמרא gets ready to bring a ברייתא that adds a bigger city and shows which patterns do not count.

keyTerms.meaning: a plague or epidemic, which calls for a fast and crying out
foot-soldiers, men able to go out to war
"and so on": the rest of the quote is assumed

phrases.english: What is a plague?

phrases.aramaic: עִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת רַגְלִי כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: A city that sends out five hundred foot-soldiers, and so on.
phrases.notes: The rest of the משנה: if three dead are carried out on three days in a row, it counts as a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי זוֹ הִיא דֶּבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story and returns to the halachic topic of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city of five hundred men with the right pattern of deaths counts as a plague.

steps.title: A large city: nine deaths over three days
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that in a city of fifteen hundred men, like כפר עכו, nine deaths over three days in a row counts as a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A city that sends out fifteen hundred foot-soldiers, like כפר עכו, where nine dead are carried out over three days in a row, has a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a bigger city to the משנה's rule. A larger city needs more deaths before it counts as a plague.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number of deaths goes up with the size of the city. Fifteen hundred is three times five hundred, so nine deaths (three a day) matches the משנה's three deaths (one a day). The days must also be one after the other.

keyTerms.meaning: the village of עכו, an example of a large city
one after the other, on days in a row

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: עִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת וְאֶלֶף רַגְלִי,
phrases.english: A city that sends out fifteen hundred foot-soldiers,
for example, the village of Akko,
and nine dead were carried out of it
over three days, one after the other,
phrases.notes: Three deaths on each of the three days.

phrases.english: this is a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: עִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת וְאֶלֶף רַגְלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the משנה's rule and applies it to a city three times as large.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a city of fifteen hundred men, nine deaths over three days in a row counts as a plague.

steps.title: Nine deaths in one day or over four days is not a plague
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that if the nine died all in one day, or spread over four days, it is not a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the nine died in one day, or over four days, it is not a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives the cases that do not count. The deaths must come in a steady pattern over three days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא now limits the case from step 27. The same nine deaths do not count if they all happened on one day. They also do not count if they were spread over four days, which is fewer than three a day. Only the steady pattern of three a day, for three days in a row, counts as דבר.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that more days means a worse plague. Nine deaths over four days does NOT count, because the deaths are spread thinner than three a day.

phrases.english: In one day
or over four days,
this is not a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּיוֹם אֶחָד אוֹ בְּאַרְבָּעָה יָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the limits of the case in step 27 by showing which patterns of deaths do not qualify.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The deaths must be spread evenly over three days in a row. All in one day, or over four days, is not a plague.

steps.title: A small city: three deaths over three days
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא repeats the משנה's case with an example. A city of five hundred men, like כפר עמיקו, with three deaths over three days in a row, has a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a city that sends out five hundred foot-soldiers, like כפר עמיקו, where three dead are carried out over three days in a row, has a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes by stating the smaller-city case, the one from the משנה, and gives a real place as an example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Put next to the large-city case, the pattern becomes clear: one death a day for every five hundred men, for three days in a row. A small city needs fewer deaths, because its rate is measured against its smaller size.

keyTerms.meaning: the village of עמיקו, an example of a small city

steps.whatToRemember: A plague (דבר) is measured by the city's size: one death per day for each five hundred men, for three days in a row. Five hundred men means three deaths. Fifteen hundred men means nine deaths.

phrases.english: And a city that sends out five hundred foot-soldiers,
for example, the village of Amiko,
and three dead were carried out of it
over three days, one after the other,
this is a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת רַגְלִי, כְּגוֹן כְּפַר עֲמִיקוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the smaller-city case next to the larger-city case, which shows the shared rate.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a city of five hundred men, three deaths over three days in a row counts as a plague.
